title: Q&A: What the EU’s carbon market review means for climate action - Carbon Brief
gist: The European Commission's 17 July ETS reform proposal slows the carbon market's emissions-cap decline from 2031, extends free industrial allowances to 2038, and expands aviation and maritime coverage; NGOs estimate the package would permit 1.4-2.4bn extra tonnes of CO2, while industry groups and some experts welcome the added investment certainty and flexibility.

themes.theme: Core trade: slower cap glide path for extended free allowances

insights.claim: The European Commission's 17 July ETS reform proposal would slow the pace of emissions cuts within the carbon market from 2031, extending free allowances to industry through 2038 (from a prior full phase-out by 2034), conditional on companies submitting EU decarbonisation investment plans.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Signals a multi-year reprieve on carbon costs for EU heavy industry, relevant to positioning in EU carbon allowance markets and to timing industrial-decarbonisation capex.
insights.locator: opening paragraphs

insights.claim: Under the proposal, the emissions-reduction cap would fall by just 3.7% a year in 2031-35 and 1.7% a year in 2036-40, down from the 4.4% annual pace agreed for 2028 onward — a materially slower glide path to zero, potentially letting new allowances enter the system into the 2040s instead of ending in 2039.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Quantifies the loosening: a slower cap decline implies a larger allowance supply and structurally weaker carbon-price pressure through the 2030s absent further reform.
insights.locator: Slowing path to reach zero emissions by a decade

insights.claim: WWF and other analysts estimate the slower cap trajectory would allow around 2bn extra tonnes of CO2 to be emitted compared with the previous schedule.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: The headline emissions figure NGOs are using to attack the proposal; watch whether it shrinks as the cap trajectory is renegotiated in Council and Parliament.
insights.locator: The proposal would result in around 2bn tonnes

insights.claim: From 2031, 80% of free allowances would go to companies that have submitted EU decarbonisation investment plans, with the remaining 20% conditioned on proof that companies actually followed through and achieved the promised emissions cuts.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Creates a performance-based screen investors can use to distinguish EU industrials credibly committed to decarbonisation capex from those merely banking free allowances.
insights.locator: It proposes that from 2031 onwards

insights.claim: Epico's Kirsten Scholl calls the extended, conditional free-allowance mechanism a 'step in the right direction' but warns it must not impose excessive administrative burdens on companies.
insights.speaker: Kirsten Scholl
insights.so_what: Flags implementation/compliance-cost risk that could blunt the proposal's intended investment-certainty benefit for industry.
insights.locator: This move is a 'step in the right direction'

insights.claim: The Commission proposes reintroducing 15% of the free allocations previously due to be phased out because of the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), starting in 2028, explicitly to slow CBAM's phase-in speed and cut remaining carbon-leakage risk.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Partially reverses the EU's carbon border tax rollout, relevant for import-exposed EU industrials (steel, cement, aluminium) reassessing competitive-pressure timing.
insights.locator: the commission has proposed that 15% of free allocations

insights.claim: Bellona's Francesco Lombardi Stocchetti warns that delaying the CBAM phase-out and free-allowance removal 'risks squandering the EU's credibility with investors and trading partners alike,' arguing Europe cannot lead the clean industrial transition just by moving the goalposts.
insights.speaker: Francesco Lombardi Stocchetti
insights.so_what: Warns that policy-credibility erosion, not just emissions volume, is a cost of the CBAM delay that trading partners and investors will price in.
insights.quote: Europe cannot lead the clean industrial transition just by moving the goalposts.
insights.locator: Pushing back the phase-out of free allowances

insights.claim: From 2029, the proposal would add to the ETS all flights departing the European Economic Area and landing within 5,000km of central Europe — a range that excludes flights to China and the US — plus private jets and other business flights.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Defines the exact geographic carbon-cost exposure for airlines: carriers with EEA hubs and short/medium-haul international routes face new costs, while transatlantic and China routes stay exempt.
insights.locator: The plan outlines that, from 2029

insights.claim: Aviation currently accounts for 14% of EU transport emissions, a share expected to rise to around 90% by 2050 because aviation is harder to decarbonise than other transport modes.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Explains why the Commission is targeting aviation specifically now: it is set to become the dominant transport-emissions source, ensuring continued regulatory pressure on the sector.
insights.locator: It notes that aviation currently accounts

insights.claim: IATA director general Willie Walsh says the expanded aviation coverage will be 'harmful,' sowing acrimony over extraterritoriality, slowing global decarbonisation and sapping European competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Willie Walsh
insights.so_what: Signals sustained airline-lobby resistance likely to shape the Parliament negotiation over aviation's ETS scope.
insights.quote: sowing acrimony over extraterritoriality, slowing global decarbonisation and sapping European competitiveness
insights.locator: The organisation's director general, Willie Walsh

insights.claim: A study commissioned by Carbon Market Watch found that extending the ETS to all flights departing the EEA (not just intra-EEA flights) would have only a 'very small impact on ticket prices and passenger demand,' contradicting airline-industry cost warnings.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Independent evidence undercutting the airline lobby's cost argument, useful for weighing how much political weight IATA's opposition should carry.
insights.quote: very small impact on ticket prices and passenger demand
insights.locator: A study commissioned by Carbon Market Watch

themes.theme: Auction revenue earmarks and a weak enforcement record

insights.claim: Under the proposal, EU countries would be required to direct 50% of ETS auction revenue toward decarbonising sectors covered by the system, amounting to more than €100bn in investment before 2030.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified capital pool for industrial-decarbonisation projects, useful for tracking EU green-capex flows and potential beneficiary sectors.
insights.locator: Under the proposed changes, EU countries

insights.claim: Despite a 2023 rule requiring all ETS auction revenue to fund climate and energy activities, only around 5% of that money currently directly supports industrial decarbonisation in sectors like steel, chemicals and fertilisers.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: A large gap between policy intent and actual capital deployment is a red flag for whether the new 50% earmark will be enforced any better without stronger tracking.
insights.locator: Currently, only around 5% of the ETS money

themes.theme: CO2 removals and international credits divide experts

insights.claim: The Commission proposes integrating 'permanent' carbon removals such as direct air capture with storage into the ETS by raising the allowance cap by the amount of removals purchased, giving hard-to-abate sectors additional flexibility and supporting scale-up of the carbon-removal industry.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Creates a new EU demand channel for engineered carbon-removal technology, relevant for direct-air-capture and carbon-removal companies assessing EU policy tailwinds.
insights.locator: CO2 removals section

insights.claim: CAN Europe's Sven Harmeling argues integrating removals into the ETS would weaken the ETS impact, undermine the carbon price and create new loopholes for polluters, and says the proposal fails to ensure only high-integrity removal technologies would be considered.
insights.speaker: Sven Harmeling
insights.so_what: Warns that removals integration could act as a carbon-price loophole rather than a genuine additional emissions cut, a risk to monitor in the final negotiated text.
insights.quote: would weaken the ETS impact, undermine the carbon price and create new loopholes for polluters instead of accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels
insights.locator: Sven Harmeling, the head of climate

insights.claim: Potsdam Institute director Ottmar Edenhofer takes the opposite view, calling the removals integration 'an important step' because it creates, for the first time, a credible and long-term investment framework for carbon-removal technologies in Europe.
insights.speaker: Ottmar Edenhofer
entities: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research
insights.so_what: This direct expert split (Harmeling vs Edenhofer) over whether removals integration is a loophole or an investment catalyst is worth tracking, since it determines removal-tech demand under the final rules.
insights.quote: For the first time, it creates a credible and long-term investment framework for carbon-removal technologies in Europe.
insights.locator: the director of the Potsdam Institute

insights.claim: From 2036, ETS-covered firms could use 'high-integrity' international carbon credits for up to 5% of the EU's 90% 2040 emissions-reduction target; Bellona's Amélie Laurent cautions these credits should be a strategic last-resort reserve, not an excuse to avoid doing the EU's own decarbonisation work.
insights.speaker: Amélie Laurent
insights.so_what: Opens a 2036-plus compliance-demand channel for global carbon-credit markets tied to EU firms, relevant for credit-project developers assessing future demand.
insights.quote: should be in a strategic last resort reserve, not an excuse to avoid doing our homework
insights.locator: International credits section

insights.claim: The Commission proposes halving the rate at which allowances are withdrawn from auctions when supply exceeds a threshold, cutting the market stability reserve's withdrawal rate from 24% to 12% starting in 2028, letting more permits stay in circulation longer.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: A structural loosening of the EU's main allowance-supply-management tool is a bearish input for carbon-price support that EU allowance traders should price in.
insights.locator: Market stability reserve review

insights.claim: EU carbon allowance prices rose tenfold between 2017 and 2021, exceeding €80 per tonne, and the Commission credits the market stability reserve with helping mitigate price shocks from the Covid-19 pandemic and the 2021 Russian invasion of Ukraine's energy-price surge.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Establishes the reserve's track record as a price-stabilisation tool, context for judging the risk of loosening its withdrawal rate now.
insights.locator: the price of carbon in the EU increased tenfold

themes.theme: Sizing the extra emissions and NGO backlash

insights.claim: Independent analysts put the extra CO2 the proposal would allow at 2-2.4bn tonnes (WWF, We Don't Have Time's Ingmar Rentzhog writing in Forbes, and Agora Energiewende's Benjamin Görlach), while German Green MEP Michael Bloss cites a lower 1.4bn-tonne figure over a shorter period and calls the proposal 'climate vandalism.'
insights.speaker: Michael Bloss
insights.so_what: Gives the 1.4-2.4bn-tonne range analysts are using to size the proposal's climate impact, useful for weighing how much the final negotiated cap might get tightened back up.
insights.locator: Michael Bloss, a German member of the European parliament

insights.claim: Carbon Market Watch says the proposal would 'severely weaken' the ETS and risk undermining the EU's 2040 and 2050 climate targets, while CAN Europe's Chiara Martinelli frames it as a gift to polluters that prioritised shareholder payouts over investing in cleaner production.
insights.speaker: Chiara Martinelli
insights.so_what: Captures the strongest NGO framing of the proposal as a step backward on the EU's binding 2040/2050 targets, a narrative likely to shape public pressure during negotiation.
insights.quote: a gift to polluters that have prioritised shareholder payouts instead of investing in cleaner production
insights.locator: Chiara Martinelli, the director of CAN Europe

insights.claim: Reception is genuinely split: E3G's Elisa Giannelli warns the proposal risks increasing both the long-term cost and the time needed to deliver the EU's growth strategy, while Epico's Scholl and Potsdam's Edenhofer see it as providing useful investment clarity and flexibility, indicating no clear expert consensus on the net economic impact.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
entities: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research
insights.so_what: The proposal's ultimate economic impact is contested even among specialists, implying wide uncertainty for anyone modelling EU industrial competitiveness under the reform.
insights.quote: Today's proposal might please some, but it risks increasing both the long-term cost and the time needed to deliver the EU's growth strategy.
insights.locator: How was the proposal received?

insights.claim: CAN Europe's Greg Van Elsen argues free pollution permits 'were never meant to become a permanent subsidy' and that extending them until 2038 rewards delay instead of industrial decarbonisation.
insights.speaker: Greg Van Elsen
insights.so_what: Frames the free-allowance extension as a subsidy-creep risk, a critique likely to recur through the Council/Parliament negotiation.
insights.quote: Free pollution permits were never meant to become a permanent subsidy. Extending them until 2038 rewards delay instead of industrial decarbonisation.
insights.locator: Greg Van Elsen, a senior industrial policy coordinator

insights.claim: ETS2, a separate system covering transport, buildings and smaller industry due to launch in 2028, is unaffected by this review; unlike the main ETS it will auction 100% of allowances with no free allocation, and a price safeguard doubles the reserve-release trigger to 40m allowances if prices exceed €45 per tonne.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: A fully auctioned system with an explicit price ceiling mechanism creates a separate, near-term cost exposure for households and buildings/transport sectors starting 2028.
insights.locator: What is 'ETS2'?

insights.claim: Ireland, which holds the rotating EU Council presidency, wants the ETS reform signed off by the end of 2026 — an 'unusually ambitious timetable,' according to Clean Energy Wire, given a prior Council document that only targeted a deal by the first quarter of 2027 for one of the bloc's most technically complex pieces of climate legislation.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer
insights.so_what: Sets the near-term catalyst calendar: watch for negotiation headlines through H2 2026, with slippage into 2027 the base case per the Council's own prior document.
insights.locator: What happens next?

top_entities: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research
